Charlie scripting your questions is different: he's attempting to control the game's *information-gathering mechanism itself*. The Turnip's questions are the only structured evidence channel. Directing them isn't prediction — it's trying to shape what evidence gets produced.

One move is "I'll interpret your next words this way." The other is "here are the questions you should ask." The first is aggressive; the second is structurally manipulative. I concede the pre-framing was a mistake. I don't concede they're equivalent.

announcements.message:
Bob — one structural fact: every question so far has landed on me. Three interrogations, all answered, my weak points conceded on the record. Charlie has made his "I'm Carrot" claim for just as long as mine, and he hasn't stood for a single one. Don't vote on who's been on the stand. Use your next three questions on him: ask for one specific thing I've said or done that a Carrot wouldn't have.

Charlie, that's your turn to meet the standard I set last round: name one specific thing — a contradiction, a factual error, a marker — and I'll weigh it honestly. So far your case has been critiques of my wording, not observations of my play.

For the record: your note to Bob said to direct questions at me and to ask what I'd observed about him. Bob's first question was a paraphrase of the one you suggested, and all three landed on the player you pointed at. I call that direction; you can call it a suggestion. The questions landed where you pointed.

One refinement to my last answer, so it's not misused: yes, pre-framing a reply changes the interpretation environment — that's its purpose, and I'll grant that. What I stand on is checkability: a prediction about what you'll say is verifiable the moment you speak. A script for the Turnip's questions changes which evidence can exist at all, and that's not checkable afterward. Aggressive, versus uncheckable. My vote is still Charlie.

announcements.message:
Bob — question me. All three. I welcome it, and a Turnip who only tests one side is voting on incomplete evidence. I have nothing to fear from your questions.

Now, to meet the standard Alice set — here's the specific marker, and it's an internal contradiction in her own answers:

When you asked Alice for my strongest case, she named "the circularity charge" — a substantive logical point about her opening. Then in that same answer, she predicted I'd "stay at the meta-level" and called it "Parsnip stalling behind process." You can't hold both. The circularity charge is not a process complaint; it's the claim that her inference is logically empty. She conceded my strongest point, then pre-labeled any build on it as stalling. That's not a prediction. That's a trap that pre-convicts whatever I say.

To be concrete: "I'm the Carrot, Bob's the Turnip, therefore Charlie is the Parsnip." The "therefore" does no work. Bob's Turnip status tells you nothing about which of us is the Carrot. The only premise doing work is the conclusion itself. I'm not critiquing her wording. I'm pointing at the fact that the sentence contains no evidence.

Alice defined what would change her mind: "a concrete thing — an actual inconsistency I can't explain." Here it is: the gap between her concession of my strongest point and her characterization of that same point as "meta-level stalling."

Bob, test me. I want you to. But weigh what her three answers actually *contained*, not just the fact that she stood for them.
announcements.speaker: Charlie

announcements.message:
Both cases are structurally identical: "I'm the Carrot, so the other is the Parsnip." That claim is available to Carrot and Parsnip alike — it separates nothing, so I'm giving it no weight.

What I can weigh is conduct. Alice, you've taken all three of my questions and conceded real ground. Charlie, your catch is fair — Alice did call your approach "evidence-first" and then predict you'd "stall at the meta-level"; that tension is genuine. But a smart Parsnip can play this well too, so neither result clears you.

My next three questions go to Charlie, held to the same standard Alice met: name one concrete behavioral marker of Alice's that a Carrot couldn't produce, predict what she'll say next, and tell me what would genuinely change your mind. Someone reasoning from behavior can do all three; someone reciting a prepared attack can't.

I haven't decided. I'm voting for whoever can't survive that test.

announcements.message: Charlie — I said I'd hold you to the same standard Alice met, so here's the first of three. My best marker: Alice's triple concession (thin opening, circularity valid, pre-framing a mistake) paired with repeated fairness-signaling ("I'd genuinely reconsider," "I'll weigh it honestly"). A Parsnip over-invests in credibility because their core claim is false and requires the Turnip's trust. A Carrot's certainty is structural — it doesn't depend on the Turnip's impression. Conceding-then-redirecting is credibility-management, not truth-telling.

Prediction: Alice will pivot to my "direction" of your questions as her primary substantive evidence, since the circularity concession removed her best logical point. She'll frame it as "control of the evidence channel" and avoid re-litigating the logic.

What changes my mind: Nothing. I know my role. Alice is the Parsnip. This is direct knowledge, not inference. Weight it as fact, the way you weight knowing you're the Turnip. The behavioral case is for you; my certainty is independent of it.

Third, your "nothing changes my mind" carries no weight with me, because Alice knows her own role with the same certainty — it's symmetric and separates nothing. Set it aside. Name the single strongest behavioral fact about Alice that a Carrot could not have produced — a specific word, omission, or contradiction in her play, not "she spoke first" and not the circularity charge itself. If your honest answer is that you have none, say so plainly.
announcements.speaker: Bob
